title: Expand social rent construction
headline: Double the housing programme. £3.9bn of capital a year.
description: Add £3.9bn a year to the Social and Affordable Homes Programme, roughly doubling it once it reaches full rate. At the programme's own average of about £130,000 of grant per home, that funds around 30,000 more affordable homes a year, of which at least 60% must be social rent. For comparison, England completed 12,198 social rent homes in 2024-25, the most since 2012-13. This is capital spending, so it counts against the investment rule but not the stability rule.

baselinePolicy.text: The Spending Review confirmed £39bn for the Social and Affordable Homes Programme over ten years from 2026-27, reaching £4bn a year in 2029-30. It could deliver around 300,000 affordable homes, about 180,000 of them for social rent.
alreadyIncludes: £39bn for the Social and Affordable Homes Programme, 2026-27 to 2035-36: £27.3bn through Homes England outside London and up to £11.7bn through the Greater London Authority.
£2.5bn of low-interest loans to social housing providers, which are financial transactions, not grant.

source.note: against 64,762 affordable completions in England in 2024-25, of which 12,198 for social rent

terms.label: Grant per home, the programme's own average

source.note: £39bn divided by the around 300,000 homes the department says the programme could deliver

rawSource.note: Extra homes times the programme's own average grant. The department deliberately publishes no standard grant rate, so the £130,000 is £39bn divided by around 300,000 homes: our arithmetic on two published figures, not a rate anyone has set.

caveats: The department does not publish grant rates: "we are not publishing standard grant rates". Social rent homes cost more grant per home than shared ownership, so a programme weighted to social rent buys fewer homes than the average implies.
Grant is not the only constraint. Land, planning consent and building capacity all bind, and the existing programme is already a step change in output.
Capital grant scores in borrowing and in public sector net investment. It does not count against the stability rule, which is about day-to-day spending.

considerations.text: Capital grants score in the capital budget and affect public sector net investment, so this moves borrowing and the debt rule while leaving the current budget alone. The £2.5bn of loans in the same settlement work the other way: they are financial transactions and do not score as spending at all.

Social rents are below market rents, so tenants moving from the private rented sector claim less housing support. That saving falls on day-to-day spending over years, is not counted here, and would partly offset the capital cost over time.
Housing is devolved. This is an English programme, so Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland would receive Barnett consequentials on top.
